Thank you very much, Sophia, and good afternoon, everyone. The 12 months of this reporting period have been marked by two very different political phases in Venezuela. The aftermath of the U.S. military invasion on January 3, which the mission has unequivocally stated to have been a violation of international law, and the apprehension of former President Nicolas Maduro by U.S. forces at that time, has provoked considerable political change in Venezuela, change which clearly has had substantial impact and consequences regarding the key international human rights concerns that are at the heart of the mission's mandate. change that has not, as Sophia has noted, yet led to concrete, meaningful indications that the country's longstanding human rights crisis has come to an end. Throughout that 12-month period, we have continued our extensive investigations to document and assess gross violations of international human rights in the country, with a particular focus on arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, arbitrary deprivation of life, torture and other ill treatment, conditions of detention, and sexual and gender-based violence. With respect to the period of time before January 3, those violations continued in a manner and at a level entirely consistent with patterns documented by the mission in its many reports going back to 2020. The scale and nature of political repression remained largely unchanged over the course of those initial four months. we continue to be concerned that likely included crimes against humanity. Political developments since January 3 have brought a decline in long-term politically motivated detentions and also in the number of enforced disappearances. Despite the significant release of prisoners over the past eight months, however, hundreds of individuals continue to be arbitrarily detained in Venezuela, enduring harsh conditions in facilities where torture and ill-treatment remain endemic. After January 3, we observed a shift in patterns of detention. We have identified the use of short-term arbitrary detention and measures of intimidation against those perceived as opposing the government, including those who have been subjected previously to long-term detention. The detentions are often marked by periods of incommunicado detention and violations of important due process guarantees. These carry particular resonance, given the context of widespread abuses over the past decade, a potent reminder to political and human rights activists that their activities are monitored and that the repressive apparatus remains in place, prepared to limit freedoms if and how the authorities may decide to do so. We certainly welcome that a substantial number of prisoners who were detained before January 3 have now been released. The names of those released have not been made public, and in the absence of transparent and verifiable data, the numbers of prisoners released remain uncertain and contested. Between 800 and 1,000 prisoners have been released between September 2025 and August 2026. The mission is deeply concerned, however, that a substantial number of prisoners, between 325 and 450 individuals, remain arbitrarily detained, an ongoing and very serious human rights violation. While the scale has diminished, the mission has also continued to document cases of enforced disappearance and of deaths of prisoners in custody after January 3. Very significantly, the mission is deeply concerned about the ongoing prevalence of torture in a number of detention centers in Venezuela. We are particularly concerned about what we have documented at the maximum security prisons El Rodeo 1 and Fuerte Guaycapuro, where the largest number of individuals detained for political reasons are held. Our investigations, including extensive interviews with released prisoners, have allowed us to deepen the evidence of the frequency of torture and the particularly harsh nature of many of the methods used, including methods that we have not previously documented, notably the use of forced intubation and catheterization, a use of a technique known as the time machine, in which detainees are held in a sealed underground cistern, forced to remain naked and in complete darkness for periods ranging from a few days to three months, and another method known as the firefly, in which prisoners were held in cells reportedly infested with rats and insects for several days under conditions of constant artificial light. Torture is clearly frequently used as a means of punishing prisoners. The most common methods include punching and beatings with metallic objects, electric shocks, including to the genitals, suffocation with plastic bags, suspension by the hands and feet for prolonged periods of time, and lengthy confinement in isolation, often while prisoners are naked and exposed to low temperatures. These methods have continued well into 2026 and were inflicted, amongst others, on prisoners who protested detention conditions after the June earthquakes. Our key observation with respect to human rights in Venezuela since January 3 is that violations continue, even if the harshness and intensity of repression has lessened in the country. As noted by Sofia, we are deeply concerned that the entirety of Venezuela's repressive apparatus marked by an extensive legal framework enabled by notorious police, security, intelligence, and judicial bodies, agencies, and institutions, and presided over by politicians, security, and military officials whose responsibility for gross human rights violations, including in many instances likely crimes against humanity, has been extensively documented in past reports from the mission. That all remains entirely intact, with no indication at this time of an intention to advance the reforms needed to dismantle that reality and institute strong legal and institutional human rights protections in the country. That is not only something of potential concern, pointing to a worry of possible reactivation. It is an ongoing and current reality as well. Violations are occurring, and absent real change, There is every reason to believe that will continue and could, as has often been the case in the past, worsen again. Thank you.
